title: Cyclotron motion: a charge circling in a uniform magnetic field
abstract: Cyclotron motion: a charge circling in a uniform magnetic field — dynamic notebook
situation:
### The objects

| name | shape | given properties |
|---|---|---|
| `obj0` | `sphere` | `mass = 2`, `radius = 0.1`, `charge = -1.5`, `velocity = [3, 0, 0]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`sphere`** — a uniform solid ball. `I = diag(2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5)` — isotropic, so every axis through the centre is a principal axis with the same moment. The only shape whose inertia tensor is unchanged by any rotation, which makes it the simplest collidable body.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`radius`** — the radius, in metres.
- **`charge`** — the electric charge, in coulombs, which is what the electric and magnetic fields grip.
- **`velocity`** — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is at its default `G = 1`**, so every pair of bodies attracts every other by `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`.
- **A magnetic field** `[0, 0, 4]` acts on any charged body through the Lorentz force `F = q v x B`.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
eom:
There are 1 body. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = F_grav_i + q_i (E + v_i x B)

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- `F_grav_i = sum over j != i of G m_i m_j (x_j - x_i) / |x_j - x_i|^3` — the mutual attraction, softened at short range if `softening` is set
- `q_i (E + v_i x B)` — the Lorentz force on a charged body
constraints:
**This model has no joints.** Nothing algebraic relates the coordinates, so the system is an ordinary differential equation rather than a differential-algebraic one, and it needs no Lagrange multipliers and no constraint Jacobian.

That does not mean nothing is conserved. Energy, linear momentum and angular momentum are still exact consequences of the equations of motion, and comparing them before and after a run is the honest way to judge the integration.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 1 body, so the state vector `y` has

```
1 bodies x 13 numbers = 13 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

There are no algebraic constraints, so the whole of the mechanics above is one first-order system

```
dy/dt = f(t, y),   y in R^13
```

handed to the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in BDF mode: backward differentiation formulas, implicit, for stiff problems. A stiff problem is one with widely separated timescales — a fast gyration riding on a slow drift, for instance — where an explicit method is forced into absurdly small steps by stability rather than by accuracy.

The right-hand side `f` unpacks `y` into bodies, computes every force and torque, and packs the derivatives back in the same 13-per-body order.

steps.title: Create the bodies
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`new sphere` creates one rigid body whose shape is **a uniform solid ball**, left unnamed, so it takes the next automatic name `objN`. The general form is

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

Its inertia tensor is not typed in — the simulator computes it from the shape: `I = diag(2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5, 2mr^2/5)` — isotropic, so every axis through the centre is a principal axis with the same moment. The only shape whose inertia tensor is unchanged by any rotation, which makes it the simplest collidable body.

The fields given here are:

- `mass = 2` — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- `radius = 0.1` — the radius, in metres.
- `charge = -1.5` — the electric charge, in coulombs, which is what the electric and magnetic fields grip.
- `velocity = [3, 0, 0]` — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.
steps.code: sim.do("new sphere { mass = 2, radius = 0.1, charge = -1.5, velocity = [3, 0, 0] }")

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`set system.b_field = [0, 0, 4]` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `b_field` is a uniform magnetic field `[Bx, By, Bz]` in tesla, which acts on any body with a charge through the Lorentz force `F = q v x B`.

The value expected here is `[0, 0, 4]`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

steps.title: Choose the integrator
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`method bdf` chooses the time integrator. The form is `METHOD <adams|bdf|sprk|ida>`.

Here it selects the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in BDF mode: backward differentiation formulas, implicit, for stiff problems. A stiff problem is one with widely separated timescales — a fast gyration riding on a slow drift, for instance — where an explicit method is forced into absurdly small steps by stability rather than by accuracy.

All stepping in this simulator goes through the vendored pure-Rust SUNDIALS translation. There is no hand-written Euler or Verlet anywhere.

steps.title: Measure
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> Analytic anchors, computed in-notebook:
> period      T = 2·pi·m/(|q|·B) = 2.0943951023931953
> gyroradius  r = m·v/(|q|·B)    = 1

The next cell sends these 2 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`2 * pi * 2 / (1.5 * 4)` — a command of the simulator's language. Sent as typed; the simulator prints whatever it has to say about it.

---

`2 * 3 / (1.5 * 4)` — a command of the simulator's language. Sent as typed; the simulator prints whatever it has to say about it.

steps.title: Measure (2)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> Baselines before running: E = ½·2·3² = 9 (kinetic only — the magnetic
> force does no work), P = m·v = [6, 0, 0], speed 3. All of them must
> still read the same after any number of full revolutions.

The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`energy` prints the total kinetic plus potential energy of the whole system. Take it before and after a run: for a closed system with no dissipation the two should agree to near machine precision, and how well they agree is the honest measure of the integration. It takes no arguments.

---

`momentum` prints the total linear momentum, summed over every body. With no external force it is exactly conserved, and it is conserved through collisions too, because every impulse is applied equal and opposite to the pair. It takes no arguments.

---

`norm(obj0.velocity)` calls a previously defined function with the arguments given. A call that fails part way through leaves no half-built body behind.

steps.title: The graphical scene window
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`scene create` opens the graphical scene window. It starts a small HTTP and WebSocket server — hand-rolled on `std::net`, with no web framework — and prints the address to open in a browser. The window shows the bodies as wireframes, with a readout of energy, momentum and angular momentum that updates live.

The window evolves its **own copy** of the system. Stepping in the notebook does not move the window, and playing the window does not move the notebook. That isolation is deliberate.

If the environment variable `POSIM_NO_BROWSER` is set, the address is printed but no browser is launched — which is what happens when this notebook is run non-interactively.

steps.explain:

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- `energy` was printed. Compare the value before the run with the value after it. For a closed system with no dissipation they should agree to near machine precision, and the size of the disagreement is the honest measure of the integration — not a number to be talked around.
- `momentum` was printed. With no external force the total linear momentum is exactly conserved, collisions included, because every impulse is applied equal and opposite.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.

**The full note from the example this notebook pairs with**, which sets out why it was built this way:

Cyclotron motion: a charge circling in a uniform magnetic field — dynamic notebook

A sphere (mass 2, radius 0.1, charge -1.5) fired at [3, 0, 0] through
B = [0, 0, 4] feels only the Lorentz force q·v×B, which does no work:
the speed stays 3 and the path is a circle with gyroradius
r = m·v/(|q|·B) = 2·3/(1.5·4) = 1 and period T = 2·pi·2/(1.5·4) = 2.0944
(grammar.md §9 Example 3; the self-checking Rust example
physical_object/examples/charged_in_b_field.rs runs this exact setup).
Watch the hud: E holds at 9 while P swings at constant magnitude 6,
and the circle closes on itself once per revolution (~14 wall seconds).

Launch:   posim_notebook charged_in_b_field
or:   cargo run -p posim --release -- --notebook dynamic_notebooks/charged_in_b_field.posim
Press Start in the scene window (or type SCENE START here) to run
and display the simulation.
The exact setup of grammar Example 3: v ⟂ B, integrated with BDF —
the Lorentz force is velocity-dependent, so the symplectic SPRK path
is not allowed here; BDF is the recommended integrator for gyration.
